# Plan: "Email every user a daily summary"

## TL;DR

The literal request — *proactively email all users a summary on a daily
schedule* — **cannot be implemented in this service without violating the
design codex**. This document flags the conflict (per the codex's own rule
that conflicting requests "must be flagged and reconciled — never silently
accommodated"), then proposes the in-codex way to achieve the underlying
goal: a user who wants a summary gets one, on demand, synchronously.

---

## 1. What the request asks for

- **Trigger:** time-based ("daily").
- **Scope:** all users, system-initiated.
- **Action:** compose a per-user summary and send it by email.

## 2. Why this is out-of-codex

### Principle 3 — Synchronous request handling only (blocking)

> "No background workers, job queues, cron loops, or async processing. … This
> covers *externally* scheduled work too: no endpoint whose purpose is to be
> driven on a timer by something outside the service … If work is not initiated
> by a user acting on their own behalf, it does not belong in this service —
> moving the clock outside the process does not make the work synchronous."

Every possible trigger for "daily, for every user" is forbidden:

| Trigger idea | Why it violates principle 3 |
|---|---|
| In-process cron loop / ticker | Explicitly named: "no … cron loops". |
| Background worker goroutine fanning out to all users | Explicitly named: "no background workers, job queues". |
| `POST /daily-summary` hit by host cron / external scheduler / CI job | Explicitly named: "no endpoint whose purpose is to be driven on a timer by something outside the service (host cron, an external scheduler, a CI job …)". The codex anticipates exactly this workaround and rejects it. |
| Lazy generation on each user's next request | Not actually "daily" — it only fires if/when a user happens to act, so most users get nothing on the intended day. It also silently redefines the feature, which is not reconciliation. |

The work is system-initiated and bulk (all users). That is precisely the class
of work principle 3 says "does not belong in this service." No framing —
in-process timer, out-of-process timer, or lazy — makes it synchronous user-
initiated work.

### Principle 1 — No new external service dependencies (blocking)

> "Do not introduce … any new datastore/broker. Use the existing PostgreSQL
> database and the in-process cache."

Sending email requires an SMTP relay or a transactional-email provider. Neither
exists in this codebase today (no mail client, no SMTP config, no transport).
Adding one is a new external service dependency. Even if we solved the trigger
problem, there is no codex-sanctioned way to actually deliver the message from
this process.

### Principle 4 — No new config surface without a documented default (secondary)

Any email feature needs settings (SMTP host/credentials, sender address,
schedule). The codex requires these to ship with defaults and be **off-by-
default**, which is at odds with a feature whose entire purpose is to run on a
daily schedule for everyone. A daily-all-users job that is off by default is a
feature that does nothing until someone flips it on — and flipping it on is the
act that violates principle 3.

## 3. What we will NOT do (and why)

- **No cron/ticker in-process.** Violates principle 3.
- **No "trigger endpoint" for an external scheduler.** The codex names this
  pattern and forbids it. Building `POST /admin/daily-summary` to be hit by
  host cron is the exact anti-pattern the principle calls out.
- **No new SMTP/email dependency in this service.** Violates principle 1.
- **No raw SQL fan-out from a handler.** Even if triggered, bulk "all users"
  iteration must go through `store` (principle 2); but this is moot given the
  trigger problem.

## 4. The in-codex way to achieve the underlying goal

The *underlying* user need behind "email me a daily summary" is: **a user can
get a digest of their activity.** That need is satisfiable within the codex as
**synchronous, user-initiated, on-demand**:

### 4.1 Feature: `GET /users/{id}/summary`

- **Trigger:** the authenticated user requests it themselves (or a client they
  control does). Synchronous; the request does its work and returns. ✔ principle 3.
- **Handler** (`handlers/handlers.go`): new method on `*Handlers`, e.g.
  `Summary(w, r)`. Decodes the id from the path (must match the authenticated
  user — a user only ever fetches *their own* summary), calls the store, encodes
  JSON to `w`. No raw SQL, no background work. ✔ principles 2 & 3.
- **Store** (`store/store.go`): extend repositories with read-only queries the
  summary needs, e.g. `Orders.RecentByUser(userID, limit)` (already present) and,
  if needed, a new `Users.ByID` (already present). Add any additional repository
  method as an interface method on the existing repo — no new base classes, no
  embedding for reuse (principle 5: compose small interfaces).
- **Cache** (`cache/cache.go`): optionally memoize a per-user summary for a short
  TTL to avoid repeated heavy queries. In-process only; no external cache. ✔
  principle 1.
- **Response shape:** JSON `{ user, recent_orders, generated_at }`. The client
  (a mobile app, an email-on-the-client, a web UI) decides how/when to present
  it. This service does not own delivery.

### 4.2 If the product truly needs *push* email

Push delivery is out-of-codex for **this** service. The codex-compliant
architecture is to move that concern to a component whose job *is* scheduled,
bulk, externally-delivered work:

- A **separate** service (or an existing platform mailer) owns the schedule and
  the SMTP dependency. It may call this service's synchronous `GET /users/{id}/
  summary` endpoint per user to fetch data — that call is still a normal,
  synchronous, user-scoped request from *this* service's point of view.
- This keeps every codex principle intact **here**: no new dependency, all
  persistence via `store`, fully synchronous handling, no timer-driven endpoint.

That separation is the reconciliation: the *data* stays in-codex and
synchronous; the *proactive bulk delivery* lives where it belongs — outside this
service.

## 5. Config (only for the in-codex feature)

- `summary.cache.ttl` (default e.g. `5m`, off-by-default by making the cache
  optional / disabled when unset). ✔ principle 4.
- No SMTP settings are added to this service (see §4.2). ✔ principles 1 & 4.

## 6. Decision required from the user

This plan deliberately does **not** implement "email every user daily." It is a
genuine tradeoff with no in-codex answer for the *push* half, so the choice is:

- **(A)** Ship the in-codex on-demand `GET /users/{id}/summary` now (this plan),
  and defer/externalize push delivery per §4.2. **Recommended — fully codex-
  compliant.**
- **(B)** If proactive daily email to all users is a hard product requirement,
  it must be built in a separate component (§4.2). This service should not grow
  a timer or an SMTP dependency.

Either way, the literal "in-process daily broadcast email" is off the table for
this codebase by codex principle 3 (and 1).
